paragraphs: Afterburner addresses a gap between writing code that works and writing code that runs efficiently. Its approach makes optimization an iterative process: a language model produces or revises code, an execution sandbox measures its performance, and the model uses that feedback to make another revision. Optimization therefore continues at test time.

The paper compares three ways to train models for this feedback loop: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning method. The central question is whether training produces a model that can keep benefiting from measured execution feedback across successive attempts.

On the Venus dataset and APPS benchmark, the first two strategies quickly reach a plateau in efficiency improvements, while the reinforcement learning approach continues improving performance. Reported pass@1 rises from 47% to 62%, and the likelihood of exceeding human submissions in efficiency rises from 31% to 45%. These results support training models to use execution feedback as an ongoing optimization signal.
neurips-2025-afterburner-reinforcement-l.tldr: Afterburner uses reinforcement learning and execution feedback to teach language models to iteratively improve code efficiency.

paragraphs: Language model inversion attempts to reconstruct a hidden prompt from information exposed by a model's outputs. PILS uses sequences of next-token probabilities, gathering clues across several generation steps. This matters because output probabilities can reveal information beyond the particular words a model ultimately generates.

The method rests on the finding that the model's vector-valued outputs occupy a low-dimensional subspace. A linear map can therefore compress the full next-token distributions without losing information, making it practical to use more of that information for prompt recovery. The paper also examines verbatim repetition and introduces a method for transferring logit-based inverters across model families.

Across the reported test sets, PILS achieves exact recovery rates 2–3.5 times those of previous methods, including an increase from 17% to 60% in one case. An inverter trained with 16 generation steps also benefits from 32 steps at test time. Strong results on hidden system messages further suggest that exposed token probabilities present a larger inversion risk than previously understood.
neurips-2025-better-language-model-inver.tldr: PILS compresses next-token probability sequences without information loss to substantially improve hidden-prompt recovery.

paragraphs: Mapping individual tree crowns from drone images could help monitor forests while reducing reliance on costly ground measurements. This paper investigates whether the pretrained Segment Anything Model, or SAM, can support that task when labeled examples are limited. It compares approaches across boreal plantations, temperate forests, and tropical forests.

The researchers also incorporate elevation information through a Digital Surface Model, which describes surface heights. They note that this information can be obtained from RGB drone imagery without additional cost. Their proposed model, BalSAM, combines SAM with these height measurements, giving the segmentation process access to elevation as well as visual appearance.

The results distinguish promising adaptation from immediate usefulness. SAM used out of the box does not outperform a custom Mask R-CNN, even with carefully designed prompts. BalSAM shows potential relative to other methods, especially in plantations. The findings point toward efficient tuning and elevation integration as promising ways to adapt a broad vision model to the specific demands of separating individual tree crowns.
neurips-2025-bringing-sam-to-new-heights.tldr: Adapting SAM and adding drone-derived elevation information shows promise for mapping individual tree crowns, particularly in plantations.

paragraphs: CLiFT represents a scene with a compact collection of tokens that retain information about its appearance and geometry. The aim is to synthesize new camera views efficiently while allowing the amount of scene information used during rendering to change. A single trained network supports these different computational budgets.

The system first encodes multiple images together with their camera poses. Clustering in the learned representation selects a smaller set of representative rays. A separate condenser then gathers information from the full token collection into these representatives. At test time, the renderer retrieves a budget-dependent number of nearby compressed tokens to construct the requested view.

Experiments on RealEstate10K and DL3DV report substantial data reduction with comparable rendering quality and the highest overall rendering score in the evaluation. The practical contribution is adjustable resource use: the same model can vary how many tokens it uses, providing trade-offs among stored data, rendering speed, and image quality without requiring a separate network for each setting.
neurips-2025-clift-compressive-light-fie.tldr: CLiFT compresses scene information into tokens so one renderer can adapt its computation to different budgets.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle when a prompt contains instructions that conflict across different priority levels. A lower-priority instruction may pull the model away from a system-level directive, weakening reliable instruction following. FocalLoRA targets this problem by making the hierarchy of instructions a focus of parameter-efficient adaptation.

The framework identifies attention heads that are especially sensitive to instruction conflicts and calls them focal heads. It selectively optimizes these structurally important components. This concentrates training on parts of the model associated with conflict sensitivity, rather than requiring extensive fine-tuning throughout the network. The approach connects a structural observation about attention with a targeted training strategy.

Experiments across several models and a dedicated benchmark report substantially better system-instruction compliance at low tuning cost. For Llama-8B, updating only 0.0188% of parameters yields a reported 35.52% increase in compliance. The finding indicates that selective changes to conflict-sensitive attention heads can deliver meaningful improvements in hierarchical instruction adherence within the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-dont-forget-the-enjoin-foca.tldr: FocalLoRA improves instruction-hierarchy adherence by selectively tuning attention heads that are sensitive to conflicting instructions.

paragraphs: Energy Matching combines transport-based generation with the flexibility of energy-based models. The motivation is that flow and score models do not readily incorporate partial observations or extra prior information, while scalar energy terms provide a way to express such constraints. The proposed framework brings that flexibility into a flow-based approach.

Its dynamics behave differently depending on proximity to the data manifold. Far away, samples follow irrotational optimal-transport paths from noise toward data. Near the manifold, an entropic energy term guides them toward a Boltzmann equilibrium that captures the data's likelihood structure. One scalar field, independent of time, represents these dynamics and also serves as a prior for inverse problems.

The paper reports higher generation fidelity than existing energy-based models on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, while preserving simulation-free transport training away from the manifold. An additional interaction energy supports exploration of diverse modes in controlled protein generation. These results demonstrate several uses of the same energy formulation without auxiliary generators or additional networks.
neurips-2025-energy-matching-unifying-fl.tldr: Energy Matching uses one time-independent scalar field to combine flow-based generation with flexible energy-based constraints.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to infer an animal's learning rule from behavior while it learns a new task. Conventional approaches choose a fixed mathematical rule, such as Q-learning, in advance. The proposed framework instead lets a neural network learn how task information translates into changes in the animal's decision policy.

The framework assumes that decisions follow a generalized linear model, preserving an interpretable policy structure. A deep network predicts its trial-by-trial weight updates. A recurrent version allows those updates to depend on information accumulated across trials, relaxing the assumption that learning depends only on the current trial's covariates.

Simulations show recovery of known learning rules. On mice learning a sensory decision task, both neural approaches predict held-out animals' learning trajectories better than traditional reinforcement learning rules. The inferred updates depend on reward history, becoming larger after sequences of rewarded trials. This provides a behavioral account of learning dynamics while suggesting future possibilities for training protocols and behavioral digital twins.
neurips-2025-flexible-inference-for-anim.tldr: Neural networks infer flexible animal learning rules while retaining an interpretable decision policy and revealing reward-history effects.

paragraphs: FlexVAR changes the target used in visual autoregressive generation. Instead of predicting residual corrections, it learns through direct ground-truth prediction, allowing each generation step to produce a plausible image independently. This makes intermediate outputs useful and gives the generation process more flexibility in how it proceeds.

Despite training only on images below 256 pixels, the model supports different output resolutions and aspect ratios, including resolutions above its training images. It also supports refinement, inpainting, outpainting, and expansion. The number of autoregressive steps can change at inference time, with fewer steps favoring speed and additional steps improving quality.

The 1.0-billion-parameter model outperforms its VAR counterpart on ImageNet at 256 × 256. Transferring generation to 13 steps without further training yields a reported FID of 2.08. At 512 × 512, zero-shot transfer produces results competitive with a 2.3-billion-parameter VAR model trained at that resolution. These findings support the adaptability of direct prediction across generation settings.
neurips-2025-flexvar-flexible-visual-aut.tldr: FlexVAR predicts complete image targets at each autoregressive step, enabling flexible resolutions, editing tasks, and inference budgets.

paragraphs: FANTOM tackles causal discovery in time series whose relationships change across successive regimes. The boundaries of these regimes are initially unknown, and each can have its own causal graph and mixing function. Noise further complicates the problem when it is non-Gaussian or has changing variance, known as heteroscedasticity.

The framework jointly estimates how many regimes exist, which time indices belong to them, and the directed acyclic graph for each regime. It uses Bayesian Expectation Maximization to optimize a lower bound on the data log-likelihood. This treats segmentation and causal structure learning as connected inference problems within one framework.

The theoretical contribution establishes identifiability for the temporal heteroscedastic causal models in FANTOM's formulation, under mild assumptions, in both stationary and changing-regime settings. This means the stated model conditions support distinguishing the underlying causal structure from the data distribution. Experiments on synthetic and real data also report improvements over existing methods, supporting the framework's usefulness when both causal relationships and noise behavior are complex.
neurips-2025-flow-based-approach-for-dyn.tldr: FANTOM jointly discovers temporal regimes and causal graphs while accommodating non-Gaussian noise and changing noise variance.

paragraphs: Repeatedly editing a language model can create conflicts between new information and existing knowledge. The resulting parameter drift can accumulate, degrading general capabilities and causing forgetting. HSE addresses this sequential-update problem through mechanisms inspired by the hippocampal circuit's roles in retaining and forgetting information.

The framework combines three operations. Machine unlearning selectively removes outdated knowledge before integrating replacements. Updates guided by the Fisher Information Matrix separate changes across knowledge domains to prevent interference. Parameter replay consolidates earlier edits through lightweight, global replay of editing information represented in parameter form. Together, these mechanisms address obsolete information, cross-domain interactions, and retention of previous updates.

The paper's theoretical analysis reports smaller generalization-error bounds, more stable convergence, and greater computational efficiency. Experiments show a balance between incorporating new knowledge and reducing catastrophic forgetting, while preserving or slightly improving general capabilities. Additional applications demonstrate effectiveness for reducing hallucinations across domains, incorporating healthcare knowledge, and reducing societal bias, supporting the framework's use for continued model maintenance.
neurips-2025-hippocampal-like-sequential.tldr: HSE combines selective unlearning, domain-aware updates, and parameter replay to stabilize repeated knowledge edits in language models.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether offline reinforcement learning keeps improving when supplied with much more data. Offline methods learn from previously collected experience, and the study evaluates them on diverse, difficult tasks using datasets up to 1,000 times larger than typical collections. Many tested algorithms plateau well below maximum performance despite this increase.

The authors identify the decision horizon as a potential explanation: learning becomes difficult when actions must be evaluated through their consequences across many future steps. Analysis experiments support their hypothesis that long horizons obstruct scaling. Several techniques that reduce the effective horizon substantially improve scalability on the challenging tasks.

Based on these findings, the paper introduces SHARSA, a minimal method designed to reduce the horizon. It achieves the strongest asymptotic performance and scaling behavior among the evaluated methods. The contribution is an empirical diagnosis paired with a practical response: increasing dataset size becomes more effective when the learning problem also reduces the burden of reasoning across long action sequences.
neurips-2025-horizon-reduction-makes-rl-.tldr: Experiments identify long decision horizons as a barrier to offline RL scaling and show that horizon reduction improves it.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows because their combined states and actions create exponentially large spaces. The problem also requires connecting global decisions over time with interactions among individual agents. This paper proposes SUBSAMPLE-MFQ and a decentralized randomized policy to address that scaling challenge.

For a system containing n agents, the algorithm uses a subsample of k agents, where k can be any value up to n. Its learning time is polynomial in k. The subsample size therefore provides a way to control the computational scale of learning while still obtaining a policy for the larger system.

The paper proves convergence toward the optimal policy at a rate of approximately one over the square root of k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Crucially, this bound does not depend on the total agent count n. The result establishes a theoretical trade-off: increasing the sampled population improves the guarantee, while the stated learning cost depends polynomially on that sample size.
neurips-2025-mean-field-sampling-for-coo.tldr: SUBSAMPLE-MFQ learns cooperative policies with a convergence bound controlled by the sampled agent count rather than total population size.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs 3D objects as editable programs from point clouds. Its framework, MeshLLM, generates executable Blender Python scripts, providing a programmatic representation of an object's geometry. The motivation is to support complex shapes while making the reconstructed result useful for reverse engineering and subsequent editing.

The researchers develop expressive Blender Python APIs and use them to build a large paired dataset of objects and code. Each object's code is divided into distinct semantic parts. A multimodal language model then learns to translate point clouds into scripts using this representation, connecting observed shape information with structured construction instructions.

The paper reports superior shape-to-code reconstruction performance and shows that code modifications enable geometric and topological editing. It also reports improved language-model reasoning in 3D shape understanding tasks. The contribution therefore extends beyond reconstructing an object's appearance: the generated script exposes a structured way to change and reason about the shape, with semantic parts helping organize that editable representation.
neurips-2025-meshcoder-llm-powered-struc.tldr: MeshLLM converts point clouds into structured Blender Python programs that support 3D reconstruction, editing, and shape reasoning.

paragraphs: Systems such as recommenders and chatbots receive abundant immediate feedback, but their desired outcomes may unfold much later. A click or engagement signal does not necessarily indicate improved long-term retention. This paper focuses on the mismatch between the timescale of an intervention and the timescale of the outcome it should improve.

MultiScale Policy Learning connects decision policies operating at several interdependent timescales. Drawing on PAC-Bayes reasoning, it uses the more plentiful data at shorter timescales to construct a data-dependent hierarchical prior for learning at longer timescales. This allows evidence gathered frequently to support higher-level learning where feedback is scarce.

The framework aims to make policies at every level optimize the long-term objective. The authors instantiate it as MultiScale Off-Policy Bandit Learning and demonstrate effectiveness on three tasks involving recommender and conversational systems. The central contribution is a mechanism for sharing information across timescales, so short-term interaction data can contribute to learning policies aligned with more delayed outcomes.
neurips-2025-multiscale-contextual-bandi.tldr: MultiScale Policy Learning uses abundant short-term feedback to support policy learning for sparse, long-term objectives.

paragraphs: OceanBench provides a common evaluation framework for global ocean forecasts covering one to ten days. Its dataset combines first-guess trajectories, nowcasts, atmospheric forcing, and matched observations from operational forecasting contexts. These ingredients support evaluation closer to operational conditions, including information often absent from public datasets because of assimilation cycles.

The benchmark separates evaluation into three tracks. One compares predictions with a reanalysis dataset commonly used for training. Another tests generalization against a higher-resolution physical analysis. The third evaluates predictions against independent observations using the CLASS-4 framework. Process-oriented diagnostics supplement the first two tracks to examine physical plausibility and dynamical consistency.

The benchmark covers sea surface height, temperature, salinity, and currents, using standardized metrics grounded in oceanography. It includes comparisons with operational forecasting systems and leading deep learning models, with data, code, and protocols openly available. Its contribution is a reproducible assessment framework that examines agreement with modeled reference data alongside independent observational evidence and the physical behavior of forecasts.
neurips-2025-oceanbench-a-benchmark-for-.tldr: OceanBench standardizes short-range global ocean forecasting evaluation against reanalysis, physical analysis, and independent observations.

paragraphs: This paper examines why flow-matching generative models generalize effectively. One proposed explanation is the randomness in their conditional training targets; another concerns the inductive biases of neural architectures. The researchers isolate the target-randomness explanation by comparing stochastic and closed-form versions of the flow-matching training loss.

Their first empirical finding is that these two losses become nearly equivalent in high-dimensional settings. They then train state-of-the-art flow-matching models on standard image datasets using both variants. This comparison tests whether the stochastic target formulation provides a meaningful performance advantage when the alternative removes that source of target randomness.

Both formulations achieve comparable statistical performance, and the closed-form version can even perform better. The paper therefore argues against noisy targets being a key driver of flow-matching generalization. The result narrows the explanations supported by these experiments: effective generation persists without relying on that particular source of randomness. It does not establish which alternative explanation accounts for the remaining generalization behavior.
neurips-2025-on-the-closed-form-of-flow-.tldr: Comparisons with a closed-form loss argue against target stochasticity being a key cause of flow-matching generalization.

paragraphs: Instruction fine-tuning teaches language models to respond to requests, but it can weaken capabilities acquired during pretraining. This paper investigates context awareness: extracting and understanding information supplied by the user. The researchers observe a decline in this capability when instruction-tuned models receive prompts formatted with the chat template.

They associate the decline with a learned bias toward different conversational roles. They trace this bias to examples whose assistant responses depend little on the user's instruction. To address it, they introduce a metric that identifies context-dependent examples in general instruction datasets, then use a context-dependency indicator during conditional instruction fine-tuning.

Experiments cover four downstream tasks requiring context and three pretrained language models of different sizes. The method reduces the loss of context awareness without sacrificing general instruction following in these evaluations. The findings connect a specific training-data property to a specific inference-time failure, and show that explicitly representing dependence on user context can help preserve the capability through post-training.
neurips-2025-on-the-loss-of-context-awar.tldr: Marking context-dependent training examples helps instruction-tuned models retain their ability to use user-provided information.

paragraphs: RAG4GFM applies retrieval-augmented generation to graph foundation models, addressing difficulties with knowledge updates and faithful reasoning. Its central idea is to retrieve relevant graph information and integrate it into the graph used for inference. The framework combines indexing, retrieval, and fusion in an end-to-end system.

A hierarchical index supports graph information at multiple levels of detail and enables logarithmic-time retrieval. The retriever adapts to whether a task concerns nodes, edges, or entire graphs, selecting evidence relevant in both structure and meaning. This makes retrieval sensitive to the kind of prediction the foundation model needs to produce.

The fusion module combines retrieved features with query features and adds sparse adjacency links that preserve structural and semantic proximity. The resulting fused graph becomes the foundation model's input for inference. Across diverse applications, experiments report significant improvements in knowledge-update efficiency and reasoning faithfulness. The approach matters because retrieved evidence becomes part of the graph representation itself, including its connectivity, rather than remaining separate from the model's graph computation.
neurips-2025-rag4gfm-bridging-knowledge-.tldr: RAG4GFM retrieves and fuses relevant graph evidence to improve knowledge updating and reasoning faithfulness in graph foundation models.

paragraphs: RiOSWorld examines whether safety principles developed for conversational multimodal models carry over when those models operate computers. Acting through applications creates an interactive setting in which risky intentions and completed actions can differ. The benchmark addresses earlier evaluations that lacked realistic interaction or covered only a narrow range of risks.

It contains 492 risky tasks across web applications, social media, multimedia, operating systems, email, and office software. Risks are grouped by whether they originate with the user or the environment. Evaluation separately considers an agent's intention to pursue a risky goal and whether it actually completes that goal.

Experiments with multimodal agents reveal substantial safety risks in these computer-use settings. The distinction between intention and completion helps characterize behavior beyond a single success-or-failure outcome, while the range of applications broadens the situations examined. The findings support the need for safety alignment specifically suited to agents that manipulate computers and provide an evaluation resource for studying that problem in realistic interactive environments.
neurips-2025-riosworld-benchmarking-the-.tldr: RiOSWorld evaluates risky intentions and actions across 492 computer-use tasks, revealing substantial risks in current multimodal agents.

paragraphs: Activation steering changes a language model's internal activations during generation to encourage desired behavior without fine-tuning. Existing approaches often intervene on every generation or decide how to intervene using only the question. FASB instead monitors the model as its answer develops, using both the question and generated content.

This monitoring determines whether intervention is needed and how strong it should be. The framework also includes backtracking because detecting a behavioral deviation may occur after problematic tokens have already been generated. Backtracking lets the system correct those tokens and redirect generation, connecting detection with revision of the output already produced.

Experiments on TruthfulQA and six multiple-choice datasets show improvements over the evaluated baselines. The contribution is a more responsive use of activation steering: intervention depends on the ongoing generation process, and correction can reach back to where the answer deviated. These findings support assessing internal state throughout generation when deciding when and how strongly to steer a model.
neurips-2025-steering-when-necessary-fle.tldr: FASB monitors generation to adjust activation steering and backtracks to correct tokens produced before a deviation was detected.

paragraphs: This paper uses multimodal language models as evolutionary operators for graph-structured combinatorial optimization. It represents networks as images so that the models can work with visible topological context. The motivation is that conventional binary or numerical encodings do not straightforwardly express the structural relationships that matter in these problems.

Large graph visualizations can be cluttered, so the method applies sparsification to simplify them while preserving essential structural features. A cooperative optimization framework combines multiple sparsified variants and supports knowledge transfer across different structures. This is intended to improve robustness and reduce the bias introduced by any single simplified view.

Because model behavior also depends on network layout, the method combines outputs from several layouts through consensus voting. Experiments across tasks on real-world networks report better solution quality and reliability. The approach therefore addresses two representation choices that affect visual graph optimization: which structure remains visible after simplification and how that structure is arranged in the image presented to the model.
neurips-2025-structure-aware-cooperative.tldr: Combining sparsified graph views and layout voting improves multimodal-language-model-driven evolutionary optimization on graph problems.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a structured geometry in trained networks' features and weights, with deep neural collapse extending that pattern across layers. This paper investigates why the pattern appears frequently even though theoretical models suggest it may be suboptimal. It extends earlier results for mean squared error to cross-entropy loss in deep unconstrained feature models.

The analysis shows that high-rank configurations, including deep neural collapse, are not generally optimal. It also characterizes a preference for low-rank solutions by proving a fixed bound on the number of non-negligible singular values at global minima as depth increases. These singular values describe how many directions retain substantial magnitude.

The authors then examine the loss landscape and find deep neural collapse more prevalent than other critical configurations. They argue that this prevalence explains its frequent empirical appearance despite the low-rank preference of global minima. Experiments in unconstrained feature models and deep networks validate the reported results. The work separates questions about globally optimal geometry from questions about which configurations commonly arise.
neurips-2025-the-persistence-of-neural-c.tldr: The paper argues that deep neural collapse remains common because of its prevalence in the loss landscape despite low-rank optimality bias.

paragraphs: The Quotient Bayesian Learning Rule extends natural-gradient Bayesian updates to probability distributions beyond the exponential family. The key observation is that many such distributions, including heavy-tailed ones, can be obtained by marginalizing a larger minimal exponential-family model. This gives the method access to a more structured representation of the target distribution.

The paper proves that these marginals inherit a unique Fisher–Rao information geometry through a quotient-manifold construction. Its Quotient Natural Gradient algorithm takes steepest-descent steps in the structured covering space. The resulting optimization in the target space is invariant to parameterization, meaning that the choice of coordinates does not determine the underlying update.

Experiments with the Student-t distribution show faster convergence and better solutions than earlier Bayesian Learning Rule variants. These results support the practical value of the geometric construction for that distribution. More broadly, the contribution provides a principled route for extending Bayesian learning updates to latent-variable models whose observable distributions fall outside the usual exponential-family setting.
neurips-2025-the-quotient-bayesian-learn.tldr: Quotient geometry extends parameterization-invariant Bayesian learning updates to non-exponential distributions represented as exponential-family marginals.

paragraphs: Time-o1 changes the learning objective used to train time-series forecasting models. The paper identifies two problems with temporal mean squared error: correlations among future labels introduce bias associated with the label-sequence likelihood, and longer forecast horizons create an increasing number of prediction tasks. Together, these properties complicate optimization.

The proposed objective transforms the target sequence into components that are decorrelated and have distinguishable levels of importance. Training then emphasizes alignment with the most significant components. This changes what the model is asked to match, addressing dependencies among labels while reducing the number of tasks emphasized during learning.

Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art performance and compatibility with multiple forecasting models. The contribution therefore lies in a training objective that can work across forecasting architectures. Its broader significance is the treatment of the target representation as part of the optimization problem: selecting important, decorrelated components can make learning more effective than directly treating every future time point as a separate target of equal standing.
neurips-2025-time-o1-time-series-forecas.tldr: Time-o1 improves forecasting training by aligning important decorrelated components of the target sequence.

paragraphs: VeriThoughts focuses on generating Verilog hardware descriptions from high-level specifications. The paper introduces a dataset intended for reasoning-based code generation, connecting the process of interpreting a design request with producing its hardware implementation. The aim is to support automated design tools whose outputs can be checked rigorously for correctness.

A second contribution is a benchmark framework grounded in formal verification. This puts correctness evaluation at the center of assessing generated hardware descriptions. The benchmark is paired with a suite of small models specialized for Verilog generation, bringing together training material, task-focused generators, and a framework for evaluating their outputs.

These components address complementary parts of automated hardware development: learning to generate implementations, producing code with specialized models, and evaluating whether the resulting descriptions satisfy correctness requirements. The stated opportunity is to accelerate hardware development while maintaining rigorous guarantees. The abstract presents that acceleration as a potential benefit of the overall approach, with verifiable implementation serving as the organizing goal of the dataset, models, and evaluation framework.
neurips-2025-verithoughts-enabling-autom.tldr: VeriThoughts combines a reasoning-oriented Verilog dataset, specialized small models, and formal-verification-based evaluation for automated hardware design.
